title: Coupled Mechanisms of Tool Wear and Subsurface Strain Hardening in Milling of Ti-6Al 4V Alloy Under Various Cutting Environments
journal: International Journal of Precision Engineering and Manufacturing

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: Ti-6Al-4V exhibits a dual-phase (α + β) microstructure in which the α phase provides corrosion resistance and creep strength, whereas the β phase enhances ductility and toughness, allowing the alloy to retain a yield strength of 800 MPa at 400 °C [ 1 ]. However, owing to its low thermal conductivity (~ 6.7 W/m·K), intense heat accumulates at the tool–chip interface during machining, which promotes diffusion wear at the cutting edges and ultimately leads to premature tool failure [ 2 ]. Although cutting environments have been widely studied to suppress thermally induced tool wear, the role of thermomechanical instability interacting with the machined subsurface remains unclear [ 3 ]. Therefore, the coupled mechanisms linking tool wear and subsurface alteration during milling of Ti-6Al-4 V under different cutting environments require further investigation.

Table  1  compares the test results and challenges from the recent studies using dry, wet, and cryogenic cutting conditions in machining Ti-6Al-4V alloy. Pradhan et al. [ 4 ] reported that in dry cutting, increased cutting temperature causes thermal damage to the tool, shortening its life and performance. While, Krishnan et al. [ 5 ] pointed out that under the same operating parameters, the tool life in cryogenic cooling is 1.9 times of flood cooling and 4.38 times of dry cutting. Wang et al. [ 9 ] explained that due to the thermal-mechanical effect, tools undergo irregular plastic deformation, leading to more severe fatigue, making them prone to wear. Under the action of cryogenic cooling, the tool edge has higher hardness and brittleness. Park et al. [ 10 ] compared the application of cryogenic coolant inside and outside the tool, finding that internal spraying of LN 2  slightly reduced the cutting force, as it reduced the hardening of the titanium. However, Gajrani et al. [ 18 ] pointed out that cryogenic environments can increase the cutting tool hardness due to the quenching effect of LN 2 , which in turn reduces workpiece surface roughness. Notably, the coupled thermomechanical effects on tool wear and machined subsurface alterations remain unexplored. During titanium alloy machining, diamond-like carbon (DLC) coatings applied to carbide tools can effectively suppress built-up edge formation and thermal fatigue, thereby improving tool life and machining stability. Radi et al. [ 23 ] developed friction and wear maps for Ti-6Al-4V in sliding tests with DLC coatings and reported that graphitisation of the coating increases both friction coefficient and wear rate, based on Raman spectroscopic shifts of the D and G bands. In addition, Boubiche et al. [ 24 ] demonstrated that graphitisation of DLC coatings occurs through long-range kinetic mechanisms over a temperature range extending from below 573 K to approximately 773 K, with the transformation strongly dependent on the catalytic environment. On the other hand, Ziberov et al. [ 25 ] reported that cracks were commonly initiated on the matrix of DLC-coated tools due to thermal fatigue. Chenrayan et al. [ 26 ] found that when the cutting temperature approached 200 °C, the DLC coating structure rapidly wore out and crater wear formed on the cutting edge, leading to tool failure. Nevertheless, Ibrahim et al. [ 27 ] suggested that the wear and crack resistance of single-layer DLC coatings can be enhanced using a double-layer DLC/TiAlN coating, because the intermediate layer reinforces the DLC layer and suppresses crack propagation. Although the degradation behaviour of DLC coatings has been widely reported, their performance under dry, wet, and cryogenic cutting conditions in machining Ti-6Al-4V remains insufficiently investigated.

The machinability of Ti-6Al-4V under advanced lubrication and cooling strategies has been extensively reviewed [ 28 ], with cryogenic cooling [ 29 ] receiving growing attention because of its environmentally benign and sustainable characteristics. Zhu et al. [ 12 ] found that while CO₂ cooling significantly reduces the temperature during Ti-6Al-4V cutting, it increases the cutting force due to material hardening at lower temperatures. Cai et al. [ 13 ] also reported a slightly higher cutting force under CO₂ cooling, attributing it to a quenching effect that strengthens the surface. Furthermore, Shah et al. [ 14 ] confirmed similar hardening, but with CO₂ causing less hardness than LN 2 , highlighting the impact of the cooling medium on material properties and machining performance. Moreover, Şirin et al. [ 20 ] pointed out that when using liquid nitrogen alone, the cryogenic fluid can effectively penetrate the cutting zone, achieving the lowest cutting temperature (~ 186 °C). Su et al. [ 30 ] demonstrated that using cryogenic cutting can reduce the friction coefficient to 0.43 between the tool and the material. Nevertheless, the effects of coolant delivery positions near the cutting zone on the reported observations remain unclear. Additional comparative experiments are required to clarify these discrepancies.

When subsurface alterations induced by machining are considered, electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) is an appropriate technique for characterizing subsurface microstructural evolution. Ullah et al. [ 31 ] used EBSD to analyze the stress-strain and temperature effects in high-speed milling of Ti-6Al-4V. The results showed that at higher cutting speeds, the material was subjected to strong shear stress and deformed, resulting in grain breakage and refinement on the subsurface of the material. Wu et al. [ 32 ] used EBSD to compare the microstructural evolution mechanisms in dry cutting and low-temperature liquid nitrogen cooling. The results showed that low-temperature liquid nitrogen cooling would cause higher stress and strain, resulting in higher lattice distortion and grain refinement. Wang et al. [ 33 ] pointed out that cutting Ti-6Al-4V would lead to significant refinement of surface grains, which in turn led to a significant increase in hardness, up to 68% higher than that of the base material.

In this work, causes of degraded machined surface integrity due to thermal softening and strain hardening will be explored. Analytical modelling considering cutting environments, tool materials, and cutting parameters on cutting force coefficients will be derived. Experimental validations of modelled cutting force coefficients were conducted by employing: tool materials of DLC-coated and uncoated carbide; cutting environments of dry, flood cooling and cryogenic conditions; and feed rates of 0.2/0.3/0.45 mm/rev in two-phase works. Moreover, parametric correlations amongst cutting forces, cutting-zone temperatures, tool wear and strain hardening will be carried out to prove their influences on material strength alterations. Postulations of in-process grain refinements and grain fragmentations leading to material strengthening will be confirmed by the examination of electron backscatter diffraction on their reduced average grain sizes. In addition, tool wear in geometrical failures and graphitisation of DLC coatings are examined. Finally, the controversial arguments about applying cryogenic conditions to suppress tool wear and reduce cutting forces will be tested.

sections.heading: Experimental Materials and Tools
paragraphs: The evaluated workpiece material was classified as a difficult-to-cut material of Ti-6Al-4V (coefficient of thermal conductivity: 6.7 W/m·K) alloy; whilst the cutting tools for the diffusion wear observations were carbide, with and without DLC coatings. Figure  2 (a) shows the dimensions of the tested Ti-6Al-4V plates, measuring 10 × 55 × 181 mm 3 , which are used to record alterations of subsurface microstructures and grain sizes in the mainstream test. The specimens (10 × 44 × 81 mm 3 ) are used for synchronised data collections. Figure  2 (b) shows the experimental ball-end mills with and without diamond-like carbon (DLC) coating on the ultra-fine grain carbide (OSG 8528410-3, Japan) tools. Fig. 2 Geometry and microstructure of ( a ) Ti-6Al-4V workpiece; and ( b ) cutting tools

sections.heading: Experiment Setting
paragraphs: Figures  3 (c)–(e) show the set-ups for dry cutting, flood and cryogenic cooling. In flood cooling, the cutting fluid is supplied at 20.35 l/min, flooding the cutting zone. For cryogenic cooling, a liquid nitrogen nozzle is mounted on a custom bracket to the spindle’s left. The nozzle, 6.35 mm in diameter and 0.3 m from the tool centre, is positioned 20 mm above the tool tip to cool the holder. To cool the cutting zone directly, the nozzle is aimed at the tool tip using low-temperature nitrogen gas or liquid nitrogen.

sections.heading: Design of Experiments and Data Collections
paragraphs: Table  2  shows the full factorial experiment (Phase A), which combines cutting environments (dry cutting and flood cooling), tool materials (carbide (WC) and diamond-like carbon coating (DLC)), and feed rates (0.2/0.3/0.45 mm/rev) coupled with a cutting speed of 40 m/min, for the evaluation of thermal softening and work hardening effects. Table  3  lists the comparative tests (Phase B) for the evaluations of flow rates and applying locations on tool wear and graphitisation of DLC under a constant feed rate (0.2 mm/rev) in the cryogenic environments. In both phases, cessation of the test was either when the average flank wear reached V B  600 μm, the cutting distance reached 3.6 m, or catastrophic tool fracture occurred. In both phases (A and B), cutting forces were recorded with a dynamometer (Kistler 9272); whilst an infrared thermal camera (FLIR A320G) was facilitated to capture the temperature field for analysing heat distributions. Data samplings for both cutting forces and temperatures were synchronised and collected when the cutting distance reached 300 mm. Tool wear and elemental analysis at the cutting edge were carried out using a scanning electron microscope (JEOL JSM-7900 F, Japan) at 10,000× magnification with the resolution of ~ 10 nm at 15 kV. Microstructural observations were conducted with the electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) mode with a scanning step of 0.25 μm beneath the cutting surface (~ 60 μm), and processing with MTEX in MATLAB. Degradations of DLC coatings were verified via Raman spectroscopy using a laser system (HORIBA Ihr 550, Japan) with a 532 nm Ar⁺ laser in backscattering geometry. Raman shifts were calibrated against the diamond reference peak.

sections.heading: Alterations of Cutting Force Coefficients
Correlations Between Cutting Forces and Microstructure Alterations
paragraphs: Furthermore, Fig.  6  shows the cutting force F R , cutting temperature, and the comprehensive grain size distribution of machined Ti-6Al-4V alloy using uncoated (WC) and DLC-coated carbide tools, under dry and flood cooling environments at 40 m/min cutting speed and 0.2 mm/rev low feed rate for a cutting distance of 3.6 m. Figure  6 (a) shows that a 10% augmentation in cutting force (F R ) was observed with the use of DLC-coated tools in dry cutting, compared to those with uncoated carbide tools. However, the DLC-coated carbide tools reduced the cutting force (F R ) by 49% in a flood cooling condition, compared to that of using uncoated ones. In Fig.  6 (b), the DLC-coated tools in dry cutting produced the highest cutting-zone temperatures (~ 300 °C) than those of uncoated ones. However, when employing flood cooling, the recorded cutting zone temperatures for both DLC-coated and uncoated tools were simultaneously alleviated by down to 40 °C. This phenomenon suggests that premature failure of the DLC coating during dry cutting may result from severe damage to the cutting-edge geometry, leading to a substantial increase in cutting forces. In contrast, under flood cooling conditions with minimal thermal influence, DLC-coated tools outperform uncoated tools due to their superior tribology cutting-zone performance. Fig. 6 Comparisons of: ( a ) cutting forces and ( b ) cutting-zone temperatures for WC and DLC-coated tools under dry and flood cooling; the overall average grain sizes with: ( c ) WC tools under dry cutting; ( d ) DLC-coated tools under dry cutting; ( e ) WC tools under flood cooling; and ( f ) DLC-coated tools under flood cooling, at the cessations of the tests

Figures  6 (c)–(f) show overall average grain sizes of 77.93 μm, 65.39 μm, 66.80 μm, and 83.45 μm with cutting conditions of WC/Dry, DLC/Dry, WC/Flooding, and DLC/Flooding, respectively. It is noticeable that cutting with a DLC-coated tool gave a grain structure finer than that of uncoated carbide tools in dry condition, owing to the higher cutting force (F R ) produced from the coupled cutting force coefficients. In contrast, with flood cooling environment, the uncoated tools produced greater cutting forces than DLC-coated tools by 49% due to the developed grain refinement was enhanced, which was in-line with strengthen material coefficients. In summary, grain size reduction confirmed the occurrence of grain fragmentation and refinement under both dry cutting and flood cooling conditions. Furthermore, subsurface grain refinement resulted in elevated cutting forces (F R ) and increased cutting force coefficients in a coupled manner.

sections.heading: Analysis of Cutting Forces and Temperatures
paragraphs: Figures  7 (a) and (b) show the cutting forces under dry and flooding conditions. Obviously, the exerted cutting forces of 600–1000 N exerted in a dry condition were higher than those of 200–800 N in a flooding condition. Using a low feed rate (0.2 mm/rev) in dry cutting, the uncoated carbide tool exerted lower cutting forces by 11% than that of the DLC-coated tools. In contrast, with a flooding condition, the DLC-coated tools exerted cutting forces (~ 305 N) were 33% lower than those of the uncoated carbide tools, owing to the presence of sufficient lubrication and cooling effects for suppressing abrasion wear. However, tests using high feed rates (~ 0.45 mm/rev) presented premature failures under a flooding condition for both coated and uncoated tools, since the excessive cooling may have enhanced strain hardening on the machined surfaces, resulting in premature tool failures. Notably, aside to the major dominant of feed rate, the statistical test results (Figs.  7 (c) and (d)) suggested that the interactions of cutting environments to tool materials and feed rates were both significant to reduce cutting forces, with a total contribution of 15.4%. Fig. 7 Measurement results of cutting forces under: ( a ) dry cutting and ( b ) flood cooling conditions; and ( c ) response surface plots and ( d ) ANOVA at the cessation of the tests

Figures  8 (a) and (b) show the temperature evolutions when cutting Ti-6Al-4V in dry and flooding conditions, respectively. Obviously, the recorded cutting-zone temperatures of 30.3–36.7 °C in the flooding condition for all tests were much lower than those of 104.9–301.9 °C in dry cutting, with a maximum reduction of 71.1–88.2%. In fact, when cutting environmental conditions were parametrically controlled in the experiment, their influences on the recorded cutting-zone temperatures surpassed feed rates and the DLC coating significantly. The cutting-zone temperatures would mainly increase with the cutting length and likely reflected minor influences to the corresponding cutting forces. In Figs.  8 (c) and (d), the response surface plot and ANOVA results suggested that the cutting environment was the solely significant factor affecting cutting temperature, whereas the low-friction DLC coating did not effectively reduce temperature, likely due to coating failure. This phenomenon implied that thermal softening effects were either absent or insufficient to counteract the dominant strain hardening response of the Ti-6Al-4V alloy, even when the high temperature approached ~ 301.9 °C.
Fig. 8 Measurement results of cutting-zone temperatures in: ( a ) dry cutting and ( b ) flood cooling conditions; and ( c ) response surface plots and ( d ) ANOVA at the cessation of the tests

sections.heading: Alterations of Surface Microhardness
paragraphs: Figure  9 (a) presents the correlations between cutting-zone temperatures and cutting forces under dry cutting. Amongst these tests, an operating feed rate of 0.2 mm/rev increased cutting-zone temperatures from 103.6 °C to 225.4 °C, and the resultant cutting forces simultaneously increased from 262.6 N to 585.7 N, indicating the strain hardening (335.2 HV 0.025 ) surpassing thermal softening (300.2 HV 0.025 ). When operating feed rates of 0.3 and 0.45 mm/rev, both cutting forces and temperatures continued to rise, with increased hardness values from 303 HV 0.025  to 363.5 HV 0.025  and 369.9 HV 0.025 , respectively, which confirmed strain hardening being enhanced at higher feed rates. Fig. 9 Correlations of cutting forces and cutting-zone temperatures in ( a ) dry cutting and ( b ) flood cooling conditions; alterations of microhardness beneath machined surfaces in ( c ) dry cutting and ( d ) flood cooling conditions

sections.heading: Tool Wear Under Dry Cutting and Flood Cooling
paragraphs: Figures  10 (a)–(c) show the evolutions of the maximum flank wear for all tests and the selected micrographs indicating adhesion, abrasion and diffusion wear patterns against the cutting length. In addition, the results of Raman shift for the DLC coating in selected tests. In the dry cutting condition, the recorded flank wear of 51.7–404.0 μm with DLC-coated tools outperformed that of 58.0–690.0 μm for uncoated tools by 41.4% within the feed rates of 0.2–0.3 mm/rev. However, when the feed rate was increased to 0.45 mm/rev, the premature failure of delamination in the DLC coating led to rapid edge wear and eventual tool geometry failure by a cutting distance of 1.2 m. These observations suggested that, under dry cutting conditions, tool wear progressively intensified with increasing cutting forces, accompanied by deterioration in the tribological performance of the DLC coating. As a result, grain fragmentation and strain hardening (~ 344.1 HV0.025) in the adjacent region contributed to further increases in flank wear and cutting temperature during subsequent cutting passes.

Fig. 10 Progression of tool flank wear and the corresponding micrographs. Cutting tests were conducted in: ( a 1)–( a 2) dry conditions, ( b 1)–( b 2) flood cooling conditions, and ( c 1)–( c 2) in cryogenic conditions with a feed rate of 0.2 mm/rev and a cutting speed of 40 m/min

When cutting in flooding conditions, premature tool fractures were prevalently observed under high feed rates (0.3–0.45 mm/rev) for both DLC-coated and uncoated tools, as seen in Fig.  10 (b). At a constant feed rate of 0.2 mm/rev, both tungsten carbide and DLC-coated tools maintained low wear levels of V B  123.0 μm and 94.8 μm, respectively. This was due to the lower cutting force and temperature at low feed rates, highlighting the cooling and lubricating benefits of cutting fluid. However, at a feed rate of 0.3 mm/rev, the tungsten carbide tool experienced premature failure at 0.9 m, while the DLC tool maintained steady wear progression up to 3.3 m with V B  169.2 μm. Although, delamination of the DLC coating occurred at 3.6 m, resulting in a fracture at the cutting edge. Therefore, it was concluded that the DLC-coated tool exerted low flank wear in both dry and flooding conditions compared to the uncoated tools, by 49.7% and 22.9%, respectively, due to the function of the low-friction coatings. Figure  10 (c) presents the progression of flank wear under cryogenic cutting using a tungsten carbide tool at a fixed feed rate of 0.2 mm/rev in comparative experiments across dry, flood, and LN 2  cooling conditions. With liquid nitrogen applied to the cutting edge, the minimum wear of 49.8 μm was observed at 3 m: 72.5% and 47.5% lower than dry and flood cooling, respectively. However, at 3.3 m, wear surged to 408.0 μm with a 719.3% increase due to coating failure under severe thermal gradients. Conversely, when gaseous and liquid nitrogen were applied to the tool shank in comparative experiments, severe cutting-edge fracture (V B  411.8–587.1 μm) occurred at a cutting length of 1.2 m, resulting from increased shear-zone strengthening, hardened chip behaviour, and likely insufficient lubrication within the seizure zone. These results demonstrated that tribological enhancement at the tool–chip interface was achieved only when cryogenic or subcooled media were delivered directly to the cutting edge, leading to reduced flank wear. Conversely, when gaseous or liquid nitrogen was applied at the tool shank, strengthening of the uncut material and chip outweighed the tribological benefits within the shear zone, ultimately accelerating premature tool failure.

Figure  11  Fracturing of cutting edge at the cessation of the tests (3.6 m), using uncoated tungsten carbide tools in (a) dry cutting and (b) flood cooling environments with a feed rate of 0.2 mm/rev coupled with a cutting speed of 40 m/min of 0.2 mm/rev. Figure  11 (a) presents the wear patterns of adhesive wear, abrasion wear and diffusion wear under dry cutting. According to the EBSD analysis results, the abrasion wear at the cutting edges produced rolling effects on the machined surfaces where the superficial large grains were deformed and elongated, leading to grain refinement and strain hardening (~ 335.2 HV 0.025 ). As a result, the strengthened uncut material in the next cutting cycle led to the rapid increase of abrasion wear and cutting temperature. Moreover, the diffusion of carbon on the adhesive titanium residues (composition: Ti 72.4 at%; C 14.7 at%; Al 9.6 at%; V 2.5 at%; W 0.3 at%; Co 0.5 at%) was recorded as seen in S 1  and S 2  spots, which indicated the decomposition of tungsten carbide and severe notch wear defects at the cutting edge. On the other hand, Fig.  11 (b) presents the tool wear patterns of chipping defects and brittle fractures when cutting under flood cooling conditions. Compared to dry cutting, the use of cutting fluid did effectively provide lubrication and cooling effects which reduced adhesive wear and suppressed abrasion wear, with a sustained low flank wear of V B  123.0 μm at the cutting length of 3.6 m. However, occasional chipping and catastrophic facture in a stair form around the cutting edges were observed at the cessation of the tests. Fig. 11 Fracturing of cutting edge at the cessation of the tests (3.6 m), using uncoated tungsten carbide tools in (a) dry cutting and (b) flood cooling environments with a feed rate of 0.2 mm/rev coupled with a cutting speed of 40 m/min

Figure  12 (a) presents the tool wear patterns when using the DLC-coated tools in cutting Ti-6Al-4V at a feed rate of 0.2 mm/rev under dry cutting conditions. At the cessation of the tests, extensive wear patterns of chipping, flaking of coatings and diffusion wear on the cutting edge were prevalently observed. It was proven by EBSD results that in the dry cutting environment, the excessive tool wear led to grain fragmentation and significant strain hardening (~ 344.1 HV 0.025 ) on the machined subsurface, which accelerated again both abrasion wear and thermal-induced diffusion wear on the tool cutting edges. In addition, the EDX analysis proved that carbon diffusion had transferred from the DLC coating to the cutting chips as seen in S 5  and S 6  spots. In contrast, Fig.  12 (b) presents the tool wear patterns under flood cooling conditions. Although the thermally induced diffusion wear on the cutting edges and strain hardening on the machined subsurface were both eased, edge chipping and cracking occurred at the cutting edges at the cessation of the test, with a minor flank wear of 94.8 μm being recorded.

Fig. 12 Fracturing of cutting edge at the cessation of the tests (3.6 m), using DLC-coated carbide tools in ( a ) dry cutting and ( b ) flood cooling environments, with a feed rate of 0.2 mm/rev coupled with a cutting speed of 40 m/min

As dry cutting temperatures reached 309 °C, thermally induced graphitisation of the DLC coating may have occurred. In Figs.  13 (a) and (b), Raman spectroscopic analysis presents the intensity (I)–wavenumber (W N ) plots of the D and G bands for tests conducted under dry and flood cooling conditions. Moreover, Table  5  provides the calculated Iᴅ/Iɢ ratios for comparisons of graphitisation across different machining parameters. The commonly centred Raman peak at ~ 1350 cm⁻¹ (D band) shifted to lower wavenumbers of 1304–1353 cm⁻¹ (green region), indicating the increase of structural ordering with reduced sp 2  cluster size in the carbon network. Whereas the wavenumbers of ~ 1550 cm⁻¹ (G band) shifted to 1489–1580 cm⁻¹ (orange region) suggested a disorder-induced subcomponent associated with amorphous sp² carbon structures, indicating the increased structural degradation of the DLC coating. Fig. 13 Raman spectroscopic analysis of the original (T N-O ) and worn (T N-W ) DLC coatings: ( a ) dry cutting and ( b ) flood conditions

In Test 7 under dry cutting conditions at a feed rate of 0.2 mm/rev, the Iᴅ/Iɢ ratio increased from 0.93 in the original DLC coating (T 7−O ) to 1.60 in the worn sample (T 7−W ), indicating substantial growth and ordering of sp² clusters, leading to degradation of the DLC coating. The pronounced increase of Iᴅ/Iɢ ratio confirmed thermally activated graphitisation caused by cutting temperatures up to 309 °C. Similarly, with the feed rate increased to 0.3 mm/rev, the Iᴅ/Iɢ ratio increased from 1.07 (T 9−O ) to 1.51 (T 9−W ), suggesting the thermally induced graphitisation and the growth of sp² clusters being enhanced. When cutting in flooding conditions with moderate feed rate of 0.2 mm/rev, the Iᴅ/Iɢ ratio decreased from 0.83 (T 8−W ) to 0.77 (T 8−O ) reflecting graphitisation alterations were less significant due to the cooling effect from the flooding environment. However, when the feed rate was increased to 0.3 mm/rev, the Iᴅ/Iɢ ratio increased from 1.14 (T 10−O ) to 1.57 (T 10−W ) indicating that the coolant did not sufficiently enter the tool-chip interface so that the cutting forces induced thermal degradation on the DLC coating surpassing the cooling effects. As a result, severe thermal degradation occurred.

sections.heading: Tool Wear Under Cryogenic Conditions
paragraphs: Figure  14  shows the wear patterns when using DLC-coated tools in cutting Ti-6Al-4V at a feed rate of 0.2 mm/rev under cryogenic conditions. When the liquid nitrogen was applied to the cutting edge under the flow rate of 0.25 kg/min (Test 13), surprisingly the wear patterns indicated severe abrasion wear, erosion wear, notch wear, and diffusion wear at the cutting edges. In such a case, the cryogenic conditions did not sufficiently contribute to the cooling and lubricating effects in the shearing zone, instead a hardened uncut surface and machining chips resulted in severe abrasion wear. The stripped coatings and the dislodged carbide grains might lead to a three-body abrasion wear. Fig. 14 Tool wear patterns and fractures of DLC-coated tungsten carbide tools under cryogenic environments of: ( a ) nitrogen gas; ( b ) liquid nitrogen cooling at the tool shanks; and ( c ) liquid nitrogen cooling at the cutting edges, at the cessation of the tests under a feed rate of 0.2 mm/rev coupled with a cutting speed of 40 m/min

Moreover, when liquid nitrogen was applied to the tool shank (Test 14) under the flow rate of 0.50 kg/min, the wear patterns showed severe chipping and fractures at the cutting edges as seen in Fig.  14 (b). In fact, the results showed that this cooling method likely failed to reduce the cutting temperature, with diffusion wear (C: 62.9 at%; Ti: 31.6 at%; Al: 3.8 at%; V: 1.7 at%) being observed and extensive edge damages. When liquid nitrogen was directly applied to the cutting edge (Test 15) under the flow rate of 0.50 kg/min, the wear patterns of relatively minor chipping and diffusion wear occurred at the cutting edges. Although this condition provided sufficient cooling and lubrication compared to that in Tests 13 and 14, the significant abrasion-wear-induced chipping and fractures were nevertheless observed aside to the high temperature diffusion wear, by the cutting distance of 3.3 m. According to the three cryogenic cooling conditions, it was indicated that the insufficient flow rate of liquid nitrogen was not sufficiently conveyed to the cutting zone, particularly the seizure zone. Conversely, the cryogenic cooling conditions strengthened the cutting chips and the uncut materials in the shearing zone, leading to premature failures at the cutting lips. Although applying the liquid nitrogen directly to the cutting edge can sustain the tool to the cessation of the test, it was not attributed to the cooling effects, but the minor lubrication benefits. The prolonged exposure to cryogenic temperatures imposed high thermal gradients on the cutting edge, leading to severe erosion on the flank face and the diffusion wear on the rake and flank faces.

Similarly, degradation of the DLC coating in terms of graphitisation was observed. As shown in Fig.  15 , the Raman spectra present the intensity–wavenumber plots of the D and G bands for three comparative tests conducted under cryogenic conditions. Table  6  shows the calculated Iᴅ/Iɢ ratios, ranging from 1.49 to 1.89, which indicate substantial graphitisation of the DLC coating accompanied by severe thermal degradation. Supplying LN₂ at the shank resulted in the highest Iᴅ/Iɢ ratio of 1.89, suggesting intensified graphitisation. Overall, the application location of the cryogenic medium is a critical factor governing the cutting environment, and improper delivery may therefore cause adverse effects and compromise process stability. sections.heading: Conclusions
paragraphs: In this study, the influences of cutting environments on the contradictory physical effects of thermal softening and strain hardening were explored in cutting Ti-6Al-4V parts. The material strengths were analytically modelled and successfully verified with experimental results via controlling cutting parameters, environments and tool materials. The adverse effects of increasing material strengths on cutting forces, cutting-zone temperatures and tool wear patterns, along with machined subsurface alterations were analysed and reported. Executive summaries were concluded as follows:

Cutting environments would alter subsurface material strengths, cutting forces and tool wear patterns. In a dry cutting environment with high cutting temperature, the tool wear produced excessive contact at the subsurface, leading to grain refinements and fragmentations, whereby strain hardening (~ 344.1 HV 0.025 ) occurred and surpassed the thermal softening effect. A flood cooling environment could effectively reduce tool wear and cutting force, maintain tool geometry stability, and suppress material strain hardening (~ 313.8 HV 0.025 ), thereby inhibiting the increase in cutting force and tool wear. EBSD analysis confirmed that with the increase of tool wear, the grain distortion, fracture and refinement trends would be exerted on the machined subsurface. As a result, the strain hardening behaviour was activated and the material strengths were enhanced on the machined subsurface. Cryogenic cooling effectiveness would depend on flow rate and application location. Increasing liquid nitrogen flow from 0.25 to 0.50 kg/min at the cutting edge reduced severe wear modes to minor chipping and diffusion wear, whereas application at the tool shank failed to lower cutting temperature and induced extensive edge fractures. The Iᴅ/Iɢ ratios confirmed that graphitisation of the DLC coating was affected by both the flow rate and the application location. A higher flow rate at the cutting edge retarded graphitisation, while application at the tool shank resulted in the highest Iᴅ/Iɢ ratio, indicating intensified graphitisation.
